hints: Your definition needs both the force and the displacement, together with the direction condition.
State that the displacement used is in the direction in which the force acts.
walkthrough: Work done depends on a force and the displacement produced in that force's direction.
State: work done is the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force.

ai_rubric.observable: Defines work done as force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force.

hints: First calculate how far the skier travels in 30 s from the constant speed.
Only the component of the 140 N tension parallel to the horizontal displacement does work.
walkthrough: The skier's displacement in 30 s is s = vt = 4.4 × 30 = 132 m.
The wire is 30° above the horizontal, so the component of tension along the displacement is 140 cos 30° N.
Work done is W = Fs = 140 cos 30° × 132 J.
This gives W = 1.60 × 10⁴ J, so the work done is 1.6 × 10⁴ J.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates the horizontal displacement as 4.4 m s⁻¹ multiplied by 30 s.
Uses the horizontal tension component, 140 cos 30°, multiplied by the displacement to calculate the work done.
Calculates the work done as 1.6 × 10⁴ J.

hints: Find the downward force on the ground before using pressure equals force divided by area.
The upward vertical component of the tension reduces the skier's downward force by 140 sin 30° N.
walkthrough: Use p = F / A, so the ski contact area is A = F / p.
The vertical component of the tension is upward: 140 sin 30° = 70 N.
The downward force exerted on the ground is therefore 860 − 70 = 790 N.
The total area of the skis in contact with the ground is 0.33 m².

ai_rubric.observable: Uses pressure as force divided by area, or rearranges it to calculate area.
Subtracts the 140 sin 30° upward tension component from 860 N to obtain a 790 N downward force.
Calculates the total contact area as 0.33 m².

hints: Relate the given tensile stress to the 140 N tension and the wire's circular cross-sectional area.
Use A = πd² / 4, then rearrange the stress equation to make d² the subject.
walkthrough: Stress is σ = F / A, and the cross-sectional area of a wire of diameter d is A = πd² / 4.
Therefore σ = 4F / (πd²).
Substitute σ = 9.6 × 10⁶ Pa and F = 140 N: 9.6 × 10⁶ = 4 × 140 / (πd²).
The diameter is 4.3 × 10⁻³ m.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses stress as force divided by circular cross-sectional area, equivalently σ = 4F / (πd²).
Calculates the wire diameter as 4.3 × 10⁻³ m.

hints: The strain energy is the area under the force–extension graph; use the two graph points at 140 N and 210 N.
The change is the trapezium area between extensions 0.40 mm and 0.60 mm, so convert the 0.20 mm width to metres.
walkthrough: From the straight-line graph, 140 N corresponds to 0.40 mm extension and 210 N corresponds to 0.60 mm extension.
The change in strain energy is the additional area under the force–extension graph between these extensions.
This area is a trapezium: ΔE = 1/2 × (140 + 210) × (0.60 − 0.40) × 10⁻³ J.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses elastic potential energy as the area under a force–extension graph, or an equivalent 1/2Fx or 1/2kx² relation.
Uses the graph values to calculate the added trapezium area between 140 N and 210 N over an extension change of 0.20 × 10⁻³ m.
Calculates the change in strain energy as 0.035 J.
